prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Cloudflare, Inc." (ticker NET), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NET", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Cloudflare, Inc.
result.industry: Internet infrastructure, edge cloud and network security
markets: Application security (DDoS protection, web application firewall, bot management)
Zero Trust / SASE network security (Cloudflare One)
Network services for enterprises (Magic Transit, Magic WAN)
Serverless developer platform and edge AI inference (Workers, R2, Workers AI)

mission.statement: to help build a better Internet
mission.source: Company website (About page: "At Cloudflare, we have our eyes set on an ambitious goal — to help build a better Internet.") and annual reports
mission.plain: Make the internet faster, safer and more reliable for everyone.

about.plain: Cloudflare runs a giant network of computers in more than 335 cities around the world that sits between websites and the people visiting them. It makes websites load faster by keeping copies close to users, and it blocks hackers and floods of fake traffic before they reach the website. It also protects companies' workers when they use the internet, and lets programmers run their apps and AI tools right on its network. Many small sites use it for free, while big companies pay subscriptions.
about.customers: Businesses of every size, from one-person websites to big banks, governments and AI companies, plus software developers.
about.everyday: About one in five websites you visit passes through Cloudflare, which is why a Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025 briefly knocked out sites like X and ChatGPT, and its free 1.1.1.1 app speeds up and protects home internet.

money.plain: CDN, DDoS protection, firewall and bot blocking for websites and apps
Cloudflare One Zero Trust and network services replacing old VPNs and firewalls
Workers serverless computing, R2 storage and databases for programmers
Workers AI inference, AI Gateway and tools for building AI agents
Pay-per-crawl and bot controls letting sites charge AI companies

result.summary: Cloudflare has a real and widening competitive advantage built on a global network in 335+ cities that proxies roughly 20% of the web, giving it threat data, traffic visibility and unit costs that rivals struggle to match. Its free tier pulls in millions of users and developers who later pay, and adding new products on the same network is cheap, so it keeps winning share; the weak spots are GAAP losses, falling gross margins and huge competitors such as AWS, Microsoft and Akamai.

pricingPower.evidence: Cloudflare deliberately prices low (a generous free plan and cheap egress-free R2 storage) to gain share rather than raise prices; dollar-based net retention rose to 120% in Q2 2026 (up 6 points year over year) and large customers paying over $100,000 grew 27% to 4,698 and supplied 73% of revenue, but GAAP gross margin fell from 77.3% in FY2024 to 74.5% in FY2025 and 71.8% in Q2 2026 as it invests in network and AI capacity.

moats.evidence: Cloudflare is the default name among developers and website owners for DDoS protection and CDN, helped by a widely read technical blog, but its brand matters less to large enterprise buyers who also weigh Akamai, Zscaler and Palo Alto.

Once a company routes DNS, traffic, security rules and Zero Trust access through Cloudflare and builds apps on Workers, moving is disruptive, which shows in 120% dollar-based net retention, although basic CDN services are relatively easy to swap.

Every website and device on the network adds traffic and threat data (115 million HTTP requests per second on average) that improves bot and attack detection for all customers, and the scale of free users gives it peering leverage with internet providers.

Running every service on every server in 335+ cities lets Cloudflare add products without building new networks, so it can offer a free tier and still earn a 74.5% GAAP gross margin (FY2025), far above Akamai's 59% and Fastly's 57%.

The global edge market has room for several networks (Akamai, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, Google), so Cloudflare does not enjoy a natural monopoly, though few new entrants can afford a comparable footprint.

Its free plan, no egress fees on R2 and all-in-one platform undercut legacy hardware vendors and hyperscalers whose models rely on box sales or egress charges, which they cannot copy without hurting their own revenue.

Cloudflare has a long record of shipping new products quickly on its own software stack (Workers, R2, Zero Trust, Workers AI, pay-per-crawl), though outages on November 18 and December 5, 2025 show execution is not flawless.
It has no exclusive asset; its peering relationships and data-center footprint are valuable but can in principle be replicated by well-funded rivals.

customers.evidence: Dollar-based net retention reached 120% in Q2 2026, large customers grew 27% year over year to 4,698, the company added more than 80,000 paying customers in the quarter, and more than 7.4 million developers use the platform; the November 2025 outages caused criticism but no visible slowdown in growth.

talent.evidence: Cloudflare has a strong engineering reputation and was named a Top 100 Most Loved Workplace in 2023, but in May 2026 it announced a roughly 20% workforce reduction to move to an 'agentic AI-first operating model', which may dent morale and its employer image.

product.evidence: Cloudflare is used as the reverse proxy by 27.6% of all websites, an 85.8% share of that market (W3Techs, October 2026), and is regularly named a leader in industry reports on DDoS protection, web application security and SASE, with a broad integrated platform rivals rarely match.

competitors.note: CDN, DDoS, web application firewall, bot management and edge compute for large enterprises

competitors.note: Edge cloud, CDN, edge compute and web application security

competitors.note: CloudFront CDN, AWS Shield and WAF, Lambda serverless, S3 storage and AI inference

competitors.name: Zscaler
competitors.note: Zero Trust secure access and SASE (vs Cloudflare One)

competitors.note: SASE (Prisma Access), firewalls and network security

competitors.name: Microsoft (Azure)
competitors.note: Azure Front Door CDN, DDoS protection, Entra secure access and serverless/AI cloud

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Cloud)
competitors.note: Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor, serverless and AI inference

competitors.name: F5
competitors.note: Application delivery, web application and API security, DDoS

competitors.name: Cisco Systems
competitors.note: Secure access, SD-WAN and DNS security (Umbrella)

competitors.name: Imperva (Thales)
competitors.note: Web application firewall, DDoS and bot protection

competitors.name: Vercel
competitors.note: Developer hosting and edge functions for web apps

competitors.name: Oracle (OCI)
competitors.note: Cloud infrastructure, DNS and edge services

marketShare.market: Reverse proxy / CDN front for websites
marketShare.measure: share of websites using a reverse proxy service (W3Techs, 18 October 2026)

threats: Hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google) bundling CDN, security and serverless into their clouds at low or no extra cost
Repeat large outages (November 18 and December 5, 2025) eroding enterprise trust in a single-vendor edge
Falling gross margin (77.3% FY2024 to 71.8% Q2 2026) as it buys GPUs and network capacity for AI inference
Persistent GAAP losses and stock-based compensation diluting shareholders about 2% a year
Execution risk and morale damage from the May 2026 ~20% workforce reduction
Regulatory pressure over content and piracy blocking, such as Italy's roughly €14 million AGCOM fine in January 2026
Zero Trust rivals Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks and Netskope with deeper enterprise sales relationships

ceo.name: Matthew Prince
ceo.background: Co-founder; BA Trinity College, JD University of Chicago, MBA Harvard Business School; former law lecturer and co-creator of Project Honey Pot

c1.evidence: Cloudflare leads the fast-growing edge network market, fronting 85.8% of reverse-proxied websites (W3Techs, Oct 2026), and Q2 2026 revenue grew 36% to $696.1 million.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Cloudflare for one integrated, low-cost platform (security, CDN, Zero Trust, Workers) on a network in 335+ cities, an advantage rooted in a 15-year build-out and free-tier funnel that is hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Cloudflare is the default choice among developers and web operators and became widely known through outages like November 18, 2025, but ordinary consumers rarely interact with it directly.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to help build a better Internet' is repeated constantly by Matthew Prince, backed by free services such as 1.1.1.1, Project Galileo for at-risk groups and pushes for privacy standards, and a decade more of it would make the internet measurably safer.

c6.evidence: “internet infrastructure, security, outages” - the impression is mostly positive among tech users as the company that keeps websites up and blocks attacks, tempered by memories of the 2025 outages.

c7.evidence: Cloudflare sells into large, growing markets in network security, SASE, CDN, serverless and AI inference, riding cloud adoption, rising cyberattacks and AI agents (non-human traffic passed half of its network traffic in Q2 2026).

c8.evidence: Its 'connectivity cloud' vision has taken it from CDN into Zero Trust, enterprise networking, developer storage and compute, AI inference and pay-per-crawl, all on the same network.

m1.evidence: Matthew Prince has long laid out a picture of the network as the computer, and now of an internet where AI agents and crawlers pay content creators, which Cloudflare is building through pay-per-crawl.

m2.evidence: Prince co-founded Cloudflare in 2009, has run it for 17 years and still owns a large stake through super-voting Class B shares, consistently prioritizing long-term network and product investment.

m4.evidence: Prince personally writes detailed public post-mortems and apologies after outages, but the May 2026 20% layoff shows a hard-nosed side.

m5.evidence: He built a curious, engineering-led culture known for shipping many products during its 'Innovation Weeks' (Birthday Week, Developer Week, AI Week).

m6.evidence: Prince is deeply involved in product strategy and writes technical blog posts, though his training is in law and business rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: Prince has championed free security for journalists and nonprofits (Project Galileo, Athenian Project) and an open internet, publicly resisting broad censorship such as Italy's Piracy Shield.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Matthew Prince at a top university was found in the sources checked.

m8b.evidence: Prince is a well-known, outspoken voice on internet policy and AI crawling, but he is not a cultural figure on the scale of Musk or Karp.

m9.evidence: Under Prince revenue grew from $431.1 million in FY2020 to $2,167.9 million in FY2025 and free cash flow turned from -$92.1 million to +$260.6 million.

m10.evidence: Cloudflare builds its own cheap commodity servers and software stack to run lean, but its sales, marketing and stock compensation spending is heavy.

c10.evidence: Its network protects and speeds up about 20% of the web and offers free DNS (1.1.1.1) and free DDoS protection, benefiting billions of internet users indirectly.

p2.evidence: Running a secure, programmable network in 335+ cities handling 115 million HTTP requests per second is extremely hard and is core internet infrastructure.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin improved from -24.8% in FY2020 to -9.6% in FY2025, but GAAP gross margin fell from 76.6% to 74.5% and was 71.8% in Q2 2026.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 cash and investments of $4,162.8M exceeded $3,270.3M of convertible notes and equity was positive at $1,620.0M, but debt is large relative to $314.9M of trailing free cash flow.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from -$17.1M in FY2020 to $603.1M in FY2025, but GAAP operating income stayed negative (-$106.8M in FY2020, -$207.2M in FY2025).

v1.evidence: For small and mid-size sites it is clearly the best value (free DDoS protection and CDN that a non-expert can turn on in minutes), but large enterprises still weigh Akamai, AWS, Zscaler and Palo Alto as credible alternatives.

v2.evidence: Cloudflare was named a Top 100 Most Loved Workplace in 2023, but it does not appear on major lists such as Fortune's 100 Best and cut about 20% of staff in May 2026.

c5.evidence: If Cloudflare vanished, millions of websites, apps and AI services would go offline or be exposed to attacks, as the November 18, 2025 outage briefly showed when X and ChatGPT became unreachable.
